findings.summary: The page load flow is a list of fragmented lines, so the step order and the wait between steps are unclear as text.
findings.evidence:
DNS lookup
name to IP
TCP + TLS
handshake
Request
client sends
findings.fix: Render it as a numbered chain or arrow diagram: DNS -> TCP+TLS -> Request -> Response -> Parse HTML -> more requests.

findings.summary: The PUT vs PATCH bullet group mixes four methods and the CORS preflight idea, so the section holds several ideas under one title.
findings.evidence: 3. PUT vs PATCH, HEAD, OPTIONS ... OPTIONS asks which methods and headers are allowed: CORS preflight
findings.fix: Keep PUT vs PATCH with the curl example, and move HEAD and OPTIONS into a separate short group or into the methods table.

findings.summary: The Headers table packs many headers into single cells with no per-header meaning, so a skimmer cannot tell what most of them do.
findings.evidence: Request | Host (required in HTTP/1.1), User-Agent, Accept, Authorization: Bearer <token>, Cookie, Origin
findings.fix: Split into one row per header (Header | Direction | Purpose), or list only the key ones with a one-line meaning each.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "connections", "exposed").
findings.evidence: Secure: the cookie is only sent over HTTPS, so it is never exposed on plain HTTP connections
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: CSRF and XSS are used to explain what SameSite and HttpOnly defend against, but the chapter never says what either attack is.
findings.evidence: "SameSite is a strong defence against CSRF; keep CSRF tokens too. HttpOnly limits token theft via XSS." CORS preflight is likewise used on page 2 before CORS is explained on page 5.
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss at first use. CSRF: another site makes the browser send a request that carries your cookie. XSS: attacker script runs in your page and can read what JS can see. CORS: the browser rule that restricts cross-origin requests.

findings.summary: The Lax row packs two ideas into one cell, and the page tells the learner to keep CSRF tokens but never says why.
findings.evidence: SameSite=Lax | Chrome's default; top-level GET navigations only; "SameSite is a strong defence against CSRF; keep CSRF tokens too."
findings.fix: Split the Lax row into 'sent on top-level GET navigations' and 'default in Chrome', and add a short reason for keeping CSRF tokens (for example, older browsers and same-site attacks).

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "registrable", "decided").
findings.evidence: Same-site is decided by the registrable domain (eTLD+1) and ignores port, so app.example.com and api.example.com are same-site, while example.com and example.org are cross-site
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet says PATCH is flatly not idempotent, which contradicts page 2's 'not guaranteed' and overstates the rule.
findings.evidence: Page 6: "PATCH | partial update | no | no" versus page 2: "POST, PATCH | no | not guaranteed"
findings.fix: Write "not guaranteed" (or "depends") for PATCH in the cheat sheet's idempotent column. POST can stay "no" there. RFC 5789 says PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent by definition, but a particular PATCH can be idempotent.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet marks POST and PATCH as not idempotent, but page 2 says 'not guaranteed', so the two pages state the property differently.
findings.evidence: Page 6: "POST | create | no | no" and "PATCH | partial update | no | no"; Page 2: "POST, PATCH | no | not guaranteed"
findings.fix: Use the same wording on both pages, e.g. 'not guaranteed' in the cheat sheet, or explain that 'no' means 'not by default'.
